extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, humor writers, and New Yorker/cartoon-enthusiasts; aspiring single-panel gag cartoonists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for single-panel/New Yorker-style gag cartoons, emphasizing idea generation, construction, visual execution, and the psychological/cognitive mechanisms that make a cartoon work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect construction / craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is a simply perfect cartoon; it’s perfectly constructed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-made cartoon pays off its set-up precisely (e.g., misdirection where the viewer expects one object but gets something surprising). Mankoff cites a Chon Day cartoon where the sequence of visual cues leads cleanly to an unexpected but logically satisfying reveal (shoe → gun). Construction includes timing, economy, and the ordering of visual/ verbal elements so the gag lands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy versus reality (permission to violate realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cartoons are either in the realm of reality or fantasy... Everything about this can’t possibly happen; it defies logic and reality and yet it leads to hilarity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons may intentionally violate real-world plausibility; the audience accepts implausibility if it serves the joke. Distinguish fantasy-cartoon logic from realistic setups; fantasy allows bolder, surreal punchlines without moral or literal consequences (e.g., exaggerated physical impossibilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poignancy / mixed emotional resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is so poignant... it doesn’t work like the others, it really has mixed resonance... It’s not funny, but to me it’s about life without art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some cartoons succeed by evoking bittersweet or poignant feelings alongside or instead of belly-laughter. Use symbolism and sparse imagery to create mood; such pieces may be chosen for depth rather than pure humor (Mick Stevens example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching down vs. punching at stupidity (making fun of an idiot)
rubrics_metrics.description: "You can’t go wrong with stupidity. When in doubt, make fun of an idiot."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting foolishness or ignorance is a reliable comedic stance; execution should keep the tone clever rather than mean-spirited. The stupidity-based gag should be shaped to feel witty (e.g., a lovely drawing that frames the idiotism as comic rather than cruel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatable, meaningful truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is a great cartoon... because it’s humor that is meaningful and absolutely true."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes that tap an identifiable human truth or inevitability resonate strongly (Roz Chast example). Ground the gag in truths readers recognise—age, loss, social habits—so the humor feels authentic and chillingly familiar when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity/defying logic as a source of hilarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everything about this can’t possibly happen; it defies logic and reality and yet it leads to hilarity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absurd combinations or impossible scenarios generate surprise and laughter. Use incongruity and illogic deliberately to produce a cognitive gap the viewer bridges for comedic effect (Barsotti 'fusilli' pasta-personification is an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered associations / combining two different levels
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is how humor works, by bringing together two different things that usually don’t go together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective gags often join two disparate references or levels of meaning (e.g., political iconography + pop-culture figure; Swiss army knife → French corkscrews). The humor comes from the small cognitive thrill of making the connection; build setups that permit a clean, surprising linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological complexity and interpersonal gulf
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is about the unbridgeable gulf between what each of us wants and how to interpret another’s feelings... it transfers to the very complicated psychological dimensions that separate the two characters from each other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue and visual framing to reveal misunderstandings, mismatched intentions, or interpretive gaps between characters. Sophisticated single-panel jokes can compress complex emotional/psychological situations into a single sentence-plus-image that implies tension or distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining associations (juxtaposition of cliché and taboo)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This takes an empty-headed cliché and adds a little bit of scatological reference. The two associations make this a great cartoon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing a familiar trope with an unexpected or slightly transgressive element (scatology, mild disparagement) can sharpen the gag. Balance is key: the additional association should heighten surprise without merely shocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-dependent humor (assumes reader background)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you read The New Yorker, you must know a little about something... And when you know all that, you know it’s funny."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some gags rely on reader familiarity with cultural, historical, or intellectual references (Einstein, theory of relativity, sexual mores, etc.). Tailor complexity to the intended audience; for New Yorker-style cartoons, higher cultural-literacy density is acceptable and often expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: "You don’t know what the guy will say and it’s all a surprise... Subversion is at work here."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design captions and visuals to subvert expectations. Surprise can come from an unexpected punchline, reversal, or re-interpretation of the scene. Subversion often mines social norms (e.g., marriage tropes) for ironic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual execution / drawing quality matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "But this is done in a lovely way; it’s a lovely drawing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistry, line quality, and composition enhance the joke; a clever idea benefits from clean, expressive drawing. Visual style should support timing and clarity—poor execution can undercut even a strong concept (Jack Ziegler example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor from juxtaposed cultural stereotypes (light disparagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bringing together two different levels of association, with a tiny bit of disparagement against the French, which is always enjoyable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light national or cultural poking can be used for comedic shorthand, provided it is playful and not vicious. The stereotype functions as a recognizable shorthand that the punchline twists (Michael Crawford example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea-first priority (idea is the core of single-panel cartooning)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The essence of cartooning, and certainly single-panel cartooning, is the idea. Getting the idea is ninety-five per cent of the battle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual originality is primary; once you have a strong central idea, execution and iteration follow. Evaluate cartoons primarily on the strength and clarity of their central conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate large quantity of ideas (creative productivity discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you don't come up with at least twenty new ideas in a week, you're out of a job."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat idea generation as a volume game—produce many concepts to find the few that are publishable. Emphasize routine, prolific drafting, and low-filter brainstorming rather than immediate polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate generation from editing
rubrics_metrics.description: "When it comes to generating ideas, editing isn't important at all... The process of creating often obscures and contaminates the ability to evaluate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinct phases: a free, uncritical generation phase followed by a separate editing/evaluation phase. Avoid self-censoring while brainstorming; return later with distance for pruning and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation and delayed evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best way is to generate ideas and then wait. With distance and time, you are able to gradually see what's there that shouldn't be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time between creation and judgment. Distance reveals flaws and strengths that are obscured during immediate production; waiting helps identify what to keep or discard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines as stopping rule
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external constraints (deadlines) as a practical rule for deciding when to finalize a piece. Deadlines provide the necessary pressure to stop iterating and submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoon topics frequently mined (e.g., bad marriages)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not when it's a good marriage; there are no cartoons about good marriages, but there sure are a lot of cartoons about bad marriages."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain everyday institutions (marriage, work, aging, domestic life) are fertile, recurring sources of comic material. Recognize these dependable themes while seeking fresh angles to avoid cliché.
